raw_case_text:
A 65-year-old immunocompetent man presented to our hospital with an 11-year history of a huge erythematous erosive plaque on his neck. The lesions developed from a pigeon's egg-sized nodule 11 years ago. Physical examination showed a reddish nodular plaque with superficial erosions, tough textures, well-defined borders on his neck in a size of 18 x 10 cm and verrucous proliferating nodules behind his left ear with no abnormalities on neurological examination (Figure 1). Apple jelly nodules were seen on diascopy. He was previously healthy and had no fever, dry cough, fatigue, or other complaints. He denied any history of contact with tuberculosis patients. Initially, sarcoidosis was diagnosed based on biopsies of skin lesions or lymph nodes and he was treated with prednisone acetate and azathioprine over 10 years. However, the skin lesions are still gradually expanding.
Laboratory examinations including syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus tests, peripheral blood lymphocytes count, microscopic examination of Mycobacterium leprae, IgM and IgG levels against NDO-LID as well as MMP-II for leprosy, acid-fast staining of sputum smear and anti- Mycobacterium tuberculosis antibodies showed negative results. The measurement of enzyme-linked immunospot assay for tuberculosis (T-SPOT.TB) and leprosy were also negative. A computed tomographic (CT) scan revealed multiple enlarged lymph nodes in bilateral neck, submandibular and mediastinum. Histopathological examination of the lesion on the neck showed necrosis and epithelioid-cell granuloma (Figure 2A) in the dermis, which infiltrates lymphocytes, epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells (Figure 2B) and negative findings of periodic acid-Schiff, silver and Ziehl-Neelsen stains. Single polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests for rpoB and hsp65 genes of the skin lesions did not identify Mycobacterium tuberculosis until nested PCR for the same genes were performed. Tissue cultures from the lesions grew caseous yellow colonies at 37 C in Lowenstein-Jensen medium after 40 days. The isolate's 16S ribosomal RNA and hsp65 gene sequence were 100% homologous to Mycobacterium tuberculosis strain FDAARGOS_756.
The patient was eventually diagnosed with lupus vulgaris. Resistance testing showed that the pathogen was sensitive to isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, streptomycin and pyrazinamide.
The patient received the antituberculosis regimen including rifampin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide for two months followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for 4 months (2HRZE/4HR). After six months of follow-up, the lesions were almost completely cleared, leaving residual scar and hyperpigmentation (Figure 3) and the enlarged lymph nodes were smaller than before on CT scan with no adverse effects during treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old man presented with an 11-year history of an expanding, large erythematous erosive plaque on his neck.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 65-year-old immunocompetent man presented with an 11-year history of a huge erythematous erosive neck plaque originating from a pigeon-egg-sized nodule. He had been diagnosed with cutaneous sarcoidosis based on prior biopsies and treated with prednisone acetate and azathioprine for over 10 years without improvement, with the plaque progressively expanding.
subjective.past_medical_history: Presumed cutaneous sarcoidosis treated with prednisone acetate and azathioprine for >10 years; previously healthy. Denies contact with tuberculosis patients, animal exposures, or travel.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports erythematous neck plaque and retroauricular nodules; denies fever, dry cough, fatigue, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Home medications: prednisone acetate, azathioprine. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Reddish nodular plaque with superficial erosions, tough texture, and well-defined borders measuring 18 x 10 cm on the neck; verrucous proliferating nodules behind the left ear. Apple-jelly nodules observed on diascopy. Neurological exam normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Syphilis and HIV tests: negative; peripheral lymphocyte count: normal; microscopic examination for Mycobacterium leprae: negative; IgM and IgG against NDO-LID and MMP-II for leprosy: negative; T-SPOT.TB: negative; T-SPOT for leprosy: negative; sputum acid-fast smear: negative; anti-M. tuberculosis antibodies: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Neck/mediastinal CT scan: multiple enlarged lymph nodes in bilateral neck, submandibular, and mediastinum. Histopathology of neck lesion: dermal necrosis and epithelioid-cell granulomas with lymphocytes, epithelioid cells, and Langhans giant cells; PAS, silver, and Ziehl-Neelsen stains: negative. Single PCR for rpoB and hsp65 genes: negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Cutaneous tuberculosis (lupus vulgaris) with reactive cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, refractory to a decade of immunosuppressive therapy for misdiagnosed sarcoidosis.
Confirmation: Nested PCR of skin biopsy for rpoB and hsp65 genes was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis; tissue culture on Lowenstein-Jensen medium grew caseous yellow colonies after 40 days; 16S rRNA and hsp65 gene sequencing demonstrated 100% homology to Mycobacterium tuberculosis strain FDAARGOS_756. Susceptibility testing confirmed sensitivity to isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, streptomycin, and pyrazinamide.
Differentials ruled out: Cutaneous sarcoidosis (unresponsive to 10 years of steroids/azathioprine), leprosy (negative microscopy, NDO-LID/MMP-II serology, negative leprosy T-SPOT), syphilis (seronegative), deep fungal infections (PAS and silver stains negative).
Treatment & Outcome: Antituberculous regimen of 2HRZE / 4HR (rifampin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide for 2 months, followed by isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months). At 6-month follow-up, neck plaque resolved with residual scarring and hyperpigmentation, lymph nodes regressed on CT, and no adverse drug reactions occurred.
